maya.text: I've scanned Maya's prescription. Veralin, 20 mg, issued in 2031.
It traces back to a diagnosis from 2029. That diagnosis now sits in three datasets: a regional analytics release, a pharmacy panel, and an insurer's risk model.
The insurer used it to price her life. Genetic results are protected. A diagnosis is not.
Sixty-four percent. I can't tell you which insurer it was. But that insurer knows exactly who Maya is.

daniel.text: I've scanned Daniel's glucose sensor. Fourteen days. A reading every minute. 20,160 in total.
Those readings turn up in three places: a device maker's partner, a research consortium, and an employment screening provider.
The screening provider used them to score his suitability for work. He never agreed to that. Not in any consent I can find.
Fifty-eight percent. It may be an error. I have no way to check, and neither does he.

emily.text: I've scanned Emily's saliva kit. Returned on 14 March 2026. Two millilitres. Her DNA.
She agreed to future studies, academic collaborators, and external research databases. That one sentence has carried her sample into three datasets.
Meridian Health Analytics is using it now, for service planning. Her consent is still active. It has no expiry.
Seventy-one percent. And that's only the latest. I've traced 1,409 uses since.
